source: Wikipedia: Hans Adolf Krebs (urea cycle section)
finding: Krebs and student Kurt Henseleit found the ornithine (urea) cycle in 1932 using liver slices in Warburg manometers. Citrulline and ornithine raised urea formation from ammonia and CO2.
numbers: Published 1932. Builds on Kossel and Dakin 1904 (arginase splits arginine into ornithine and urea). Called the first metabolic cycle found.
limits: Encyclopedia summary. Page text read to char 100000 of 116561. It calls citrulline a catalyst, which is loose.
agent_relevance: The cycle idea came as a structure hypothesis, not one data point. An agent log should record when a structure hypothesis first appears.

source: Wikipedia: Hans Adolf Krebs (historiography citations)
finding: The page names the notebook-based reconstructions: Holmes 1980 paper and 1991 biography; Grasshoff and May 2003 computer reconstruction of the Krebs-Henseleit notebooks; Nickelsen and Grasshoff 2009 on error in experimental research.
numbers: Three separate reconstructions of one episode: a historian, a computational one, and an error analysis.
limits: The page does not describe their findings. Findings are not verified here.
agent_relevance: Same notebooks, three methods: a good test bed for whether different analysts read an agent trace the same way.

source: Wikipedia: Frederic Lawrence Holmes
finding: Holmes began with Claude Bernard's 1840s notebooks (PhD, Harvard 1962), then used Krebs's lab books plus detailed interviews with Krebs. He used the same two-source method for Meselson and Stahl.
numbers: Hans Krebs vol 1 (1991, 1900-1933) and vol 2 (1993, 1933-1937). Holmes died 2003.
limits: One historian's reading. No inter-rater check reported on this page.
agent_relevance: Founding method is notebook plus later interview. The agent analogue is a trace plus a post-hoc self-report, and those can differ (see Turpin).

source: Wikipedia: Howard Gruber
finding: Gruber's Darwin on Man (1974) treats Darwin as working in a network of enterprise: several long projects at once. The page says creativity is purposeful work.
numbers: Named Phi Beta Kappa Science Book of the Year 1974.
limits: Page does not mention the notebooks and gives no numbers. Single case.
agent_relevance: Parallel threads, not one straight line. A single state path may under-model long tasks with several live threads.

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (KEKADA)
finding: KEKADA is a program built from Holmes's Krebs reconstruction. From memory: when a result is surprising, it focuses on the surprise and sets a new goal. It reproduced main steps of the ornithine work in simulation.
numbers: Not verified this session (publisher returned 403).
limits: Not opened. Fit shown on one case built from the same story, so it may be over-fitted to it.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct template for S6 impasse: a surprise triggers a focused follow-up, not a restart.

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1990) Experimentation in machine discovery
finding: Follow-up chapter extending the KEKADA approach. From memory it argues surprise-driven goal change is a general discovery heuristic.
numbers: No numbers checked.
limits: Not opened. Claims unverified.
agent_relevance: Same as KEKADA; weak independent evidence.

source: Grasshoff and May (2003) Reconstruction of the Krebs-Henseleit work from the notebooks
finding: Named on the Krebs page as a computer reconstruction of the notebooks. It is the nearest thing to a second reading of Holmes's account. Its content was not read.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Only its existence is confirmed (via the Krebs page). Original not opened.
agent_relevance: If two methods agree on the step order, that order is a safer design source for S6 and S9.

source: Nickelsen and Grasshoff (2009) Concepts from the Test Tube: error in experimental research
finding: Named on the Krebs page as a study of error in experimental work, using the Krebs episode. Content not read.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Only its existence is confirmed. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Looking back (S9) in the real case involved finding mistakes. Compare with LLM self-correction below.

source: Dunbar (1997) How scientists think: on-line creativity and conceptual change in science (in vivo study of molecular biology labs)
finding: From memory only: lab meeting recordings showed scientists meet unexpected results often, and first suspect method error, then change the model. Exact rates not confirmed.
numbers: Figures not verified. Treat as unconfirmed memory.
limits: Not opened. A small number of labs in one field.
agent_relevance: A real surprise-handling order: blame method first, then change the model. Fits G1 and G2 if confirmed.

source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Dual space search during scientific reasoning
finding: From memory: subjects searched an experiment space and a hypothesis space, with different people favouring one or the other.
numbers: Sample sizes and rates not verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Two search spaces map onto hypothesis versus test states.

source: Tweney (1985) Faraday's discovery of induction: a cognitive approach (diary study)
finding: From memory: cognitive reading of Faraday's diaries, showing parallel lines of work and both confirming and disconfirming tests.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Single case, historian-coded.
agent_relevance: Another notebook-based case to cross-check the operator order.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: a virtual environment for developing and evaluating automated scientific discovery agents
finding: Benchmark of 120 tasks in 8 topics, each at 3 difficulty levels. Expert human scientists did far better than baseline LLM agents on full discovery.
numbers: 11 human scientists (MSc or PhD). Human completion 66% average, knowledge score 55%, 11 of 16 human tasks above 60%. Best agent (ReAct) completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Hypothesizer found 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge. Unit-test tasks: agent completion 60%+.
quote: current agents are competent at many of the components of scientific discovery
limits: Humans recruited on a freelance platform; some tasks had few players. Agents handle parts but fail at chaining.
agent_relevance: Parts work, chaining fails. Supports step-level checks and counted transitions over free-running agents.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: score table by difficulty
finding: Completion barely falls from easy to challenge, but knowledge discovery falls sharply.
numbers: ReAct column (completion, process, knowledge): easy 0.59/0.38/0.25, normal 0.63/0.18/0.14, challenge 0.63/0.18/0.10. Human average 0.79/0.66/0.55.
limits: Column labels read from layout text. Check the paper before quoting.
agent_relevance: An agent can finish without gaining the explanation. Track explained knowledge, not only task success.

source: Chen et al. (2024) ScienceAgentBench
finding: 102 tasks from 44 peer-reviewed papers, checked by 9 experts. Agents solve few. Execution feedback matters.
numbers: Best non-o1 agent: Claude-3.5-Sonnet with self-debug 32.4% success without expert knowledge, 34.3% with. o1-preview with direct prompting and self-debug 42.2% at over 10 times the cost. 3 attempts per task.
limits: Binary success against a script output; 3 samples averaged.
agent_relevance: Real run output (execution feedback) helped most. Matches G2.

source: Chen et al. (2024) ScienceAgentBench: agent design comparison
finding: A simple self-debug loop beat the heavy OpenHands CodeAct agent at a fraction of the cost.
numbers: Claude-3.5-Sonnet without expert knowledge: self-debug 32.4% vs OpenHands 21.6% (10.8 points more); cost $0.057 vs $0.958 per task, about 17 times less.
quote: LLM-based agents do not always benefit from a large action space with complex tools
limits: 2024 API prices. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: A bigger action space was not better. Keep the operator set small (section 4b).

source: Laurent et al. (2024) LAB-Bench: measuring capabilities of language models for biology research
finding: 2,400+ multiple-choice items on practical biology research. ProtocolQA uses published protocols altered by a changed or omitted step; the model must say how to fix the failed outcome.
numbers: ProtocolQA 135 questions with 100% human coverage; SeqQA 750 questions, 64% human coverage; 41 Cloning Scenarios. TableQA was easiest. FigQA near random precision for all models except Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Models often refused SuppQA and DbQA.
limits: Multiple choice, not real lab work. Human baseline on a subset. Bar-chart scores not read digit by digit.
agent_relevance: ProtocolQA is a notebook-debugging test: find the step that explains a failed outcome. A cheap probe for S6.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: towards fully automated open-ended scientific discovery
finding: Pipeline writes ideas, code, runs and papers. The authors list failure modes from their own logs.
numbers: Cost about $10-15 per paper; about 50 ideas per run, 12 hours on 8 H100s. Average accepted NeurIPS paper scores about 6; selected generated papers scored 3 to 5 by the automated reviewer.
quote: The AI Scientist occasionally makes critical errors when writing and evaluating results
limits: Reviewer is an LLM and novelty is self-assessed by each model. Authors say do not take content at face value.
agent_relevance: Same as above: results must be tied to stored real output.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: documented failure modes
finding: Failures: very similar ideas across runs, wrong implementations, hallucinated whole ablation tables, wrong comparison of two numbers, unfair comparison after a metric change, invented hardware facts.
numbers: Qualitative list. Fix used: instruct it to include only results it observed, and store copies of all executed files.
limits: No failure rates in this section.
agent_relevance: Fits G2 and G3. Keep an immutable run log, an agent lab notebook written by code.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind review: AI ideas rated more novel than human expert ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition. Novelty mean: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p<0.05). 79 reviewers.
limits: Ideas only, never executed. Reviewer agreement was low (next line).
agent_relevance: Novelty from LLMs is easy. Diversity and checking are the bottlenecks.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024): diversity collapse and weak LLM judges
finding: Scaling idea generation gave repeats. LLM evaluators agreed with experts less than experts agreed with each other.
numbers: Of 4000 seed ideas only about 200 were non-duplicates (about 5%). Human inter-reviewer balanced accuracy 56.1%; best LLM judge (Claude-3.5 pairwise) 53.3%; GPT-4o direct 50.0%, pairwise 45.0%. Benchmarks: NeurIPS 2021 66.0%, ICLR 2024 71.9%.
limits: Idea review is subjective; base agreement is low.
agent_relevance: Do not let a model judge ideas alone (G5). More samples do not give more diversity (G4).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: With oracle correctness labels, self-correction helps. Without them (intrinsic), it hurts or does nothing.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) and 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 and 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 and 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 and 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 and 43.0. GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Test sets of about 200 (100 for HotpotQA). 2023 models. Table read from layout text.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2: revise only from real output. Look back (S9) needs an external check.

source: Huang et al. (2024): oracle labels versus true self-correction
finding: Earlier positive self-correction results used ground truth to decide whether to correct. Gains vanish without it.
numbers: With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0.
limits: My reading of an ambiguous table layout; row assignment is a best guess consistent with Table 3.
agent_relevance: Explains why reflection loops look good in papers and bad in deployment.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: benchmarking progress in automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: 10 environments from psychology to ecology. Experiment quality is scored by expected information gain; theory quality by how well the explanation helps another agent predict.
numbers: Abstract only: 32B models beat 7B; closed models mostly beat open; all approaches struggle at both design and discovery.
limits: Only abstract and setup read. No per-model figures extracted.
agent_relevance: A measurable hypothesis, experiment, revise loop. A direct test bed for S6.

source: Chan et al. (2024) MLE-bench
finding: Agents on 75 Kaggle competitions. More tries help a lot.
numbers: o1-preview with scaffolding reaches at least a bronze medal in 16.9% of competitions; with 8 attempts (pass@8) 34.1%.
limits: Kaggle format; contamination concerns noted by authors.
agent_relevance: Repeated attempts with real scores help, but G4 says samples from one model are correlated.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language models don't always say what they think: unfaithful explanations in chain-of-thought
finding: Chain-of-thought text can hide the real reason for an answer. Biasing features in the prompt change answers but go unmentioned.
numbers: Accuracy dropped by as much as 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks when biased toward wrong answers (GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0).
quote: CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction
limits: 2023 models; biased prompts are artificial.
agent_relevance: Warning for notebook-style analysis of agent traces: written steps are not a reliable record of the decision. Log code-level facts, not model prose.

source: Synthesis: rival readings of a reconstructed step order
finding: Rival explanations: (a) the historian imposes a tidy story, (b) the scientist later recalls a tidier order, (c) the notebook is a true contemporary record. Only (c) is protected by a document made at the time.
numbers: Holmes combined notebooks with interviews; Grasshoff and May re-derived steps by program. No inter-rater statistic found in the sources I opened.
limits: This is my reading, not a measured result. No failed replication of the Holmes or Gruber method was found because searches were rate-limited.
agent_relevance: Use a code-written log as the agent's notebook and compare it with any self-report.

source: Gap note: LLM studies that rebuild operator order from lab notebooks
finding: One arXiv search returned no results. I found no 2020-2026 LLM study that rebuilds a scientist's step order from a notebook and measures it.
numbers: Zero hits on one query. Other searches were blocked (WebSearch budget used, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv API all returned 429).
limits: Absence is weak evidence: few queries.
agent_relevance: DiscoveryWorld, BoxingGym and LAB-Bench ProtocolQA are the nearest proxies.
